# 2020 Census

The U.S. Census Bureau released 2020 Census apportionment results on April 26, 2021.

According to these results, Arizona's total resident population as of April 1, 2020 was 7,151,502. The apportionment population used for Arizona was 7,158,923. This includes Arizona's resident population plus a count of the U.S. military personnel and federal civilian employees living outside the United States (and their dependents living with them) who can be allocated to Arizona as their home state.

For more details and data tables, please visit the [U.S. Census Bureau's 2020 Census Apportionment Results page](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2020/dec/2020-apportionment-data.html).

On August 12, 2021, the U.S. Census Bureau released the 2020 Census redistricting data files, also known as the Public Law (P.L.) 94-171 files, in the legacy format. On September 21, 2023 , the Census Bureau released the 2020 Census Detailed Demographic and Housing Characteristics File A (Detailed DHC-A). The data set contains data compiled from the questions on race, ethnicity, sex, and age asked of all people in the 2020 Census. It includes population counts and sex and age statistics for detailed race and ethnic groups and American Indian and Alaska Native tribes and villages. The Detailed DHC-A uses an adaptive design to determine the amount of data a detailed racial/ethnic group receives based on population threshold and geography level. The number of age categories a group is eligible for is also dependent on their population at a given geography. Therefore, not all racial/ethnic groups are present in all tables. Each table also has a different level of accuracy. Due to the adaptive design, there are limitations on how data can accurately be aggregated across racial/ethnic groups and geographies. Information on how to use the data can be found in the [technical documentation](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2023/dec/2020-census-detailed-dhc-a.html#data).

*   [2020 Detailed DHC-A - Arizona](https://oeo.az.gov/sites/default/files/data/census/ddhca2020_arizona.xlsx)
*   [2020 Detailed DHC-A - Arizona Counties](https://oeo.az.gov/sites/default/files/data/census/Accessible_Files/DDHCA2020_AZCounties_Accessible.xlsx)

On August 1, 2024, the Census Bureau released the 2020 Census Detailed Demographic and Housing Characteristics File B (Detailed DHC-B). The file includes 2020 Census counts of households, along with information on household type and tenure (whether the home is owned or rented) for 300 detailed race and ethnicity groups and 1,187 American Indian and Alaska Native tribes and villages. The Detailed DHC-B provides household information based on the race or ethnicity of the householder (the first adult in a household for whom census responses were provided). The Detailed DHC-B data are available for the nation, states, counties, places, census tracts and American Indian, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian (AIANNH) areas. The Arizona State Demographer’s Office tabulated the data for the State of Arizona and its counties.

On September 21, 2023 , the Census Bureau released the 2020 Census Detailed Demographic and Housing Characteristics File A (Detailed DHC-A). The data set contains data compiled from the questions on race, ethnicity, sex, and age asked of all people in the 2020 Census. It includes population counts and sex and age statistics for detailed race and ethnic groups and American Indian and Alaska Native tribes and villages. The Detailed DHC-A uses an adaptive design to determine the amount of data a detailed racial/ethnic group receives based on population threshold and geography level. The number of age categories a group is eligible for is also dependent on their population at a given geography. Therefore, not all racial/ethnic groups are present in all tables. Each table also has a different level of accuracy. Due to the adaptive design, there are limitations on how data can accurately be aggregated across racial/ethnic groups and geographies. Information on how to use the data can be found in the [technical documentation](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2023/dec/2020-census-detailed-dhc-a.html#data).

*   [2020 Detailed DHC-A - Arizona Counties](https://oeo.az.gov/sites/default/files/data/census/Accessible_Files/DDHCA2020_AZCounties_Accessible.xlsx)

On August 1, 2024, the Census Bureau released the 2020 Census Detailed Demographic and Housing Characteristics File B (Detailed DHC-B). The file includes 2020 Census counts of households, along with information on household type and tenure (whether the home is owned or rented) for 300 detailed race and ethnicity groups and 1,187 American Indian and Alaska Native tribes and villages. The Detailed DHC-B provides household information based on the race or ethnicity of the householder (the first adult in a household for whom census responses were provided). The Detailed DHC-B data are available for the nation, states, counties, places, census tracts and American Indian, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian (AIANNH) areas. The Arizona State Demographer’s Office tabulated the data for the State of Arizona and its counties.

## Summary

This layer contains the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2020 Census Demographic and Housing Characteristics information about total population counts by urban/rural status, age, and race groups at the block group level in the United States and Puerto Rico. The data is obtained via Esri Demographics.

This layer shows total population count for each block group in the United States, made available by Esri Demographics. The data is originally from from the U.S. Census Bureau 2020 Census Demographic and Housing Characteristics. Popups for each block group were customized to provide additional detail about population count by different categories:

*   Urban vs. rural
*   Race/ethnicity
*   Age groups

[**From the U.S. Census Bureau:**](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/about/glossary.html#par_textimage_13)

**"Block Groups (BGs)** are statistical divisions of census tracts, are generally defined to contain between 600 and 3,000 people, and are used to present data and control block numbering. A block group consists of clusters of blocks within the same census tract that have the same first digit of their four-digit census block number.

**Census Tracts** are small, relatively permanent statistical subdivisions of a county or statistically equivalent entity that can be updated by local participants prior to each decennial census as part of the Census Bureau’s Participant Statistical Areas Program (PSAP). The Census Bureau delineates census tracts in situations where no local participant responded or where state, local, or tribal governments declined to participate. The primary purpose of census tracts is to provide a stable set of geographic units for the presentation of statistical data.

Census tracts generally have a population size between 1,200 and 8,000 people, with an optimum size of 4,000 people."

## Summary

This layer contains the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2020 Census Demographic and Housing Characteristics information about total population counts by urban/rural status, age, and race groups at the block group level in the United States and Puerto Rico. The data is obtained via Esri Demographics.

This layer shows total population count for each block group in the United States, made available by Esri Demographics. The data is originally from from the U.S. Census Bureau 2020 Census Demographic and Housing Characteristics. Popups for each block group were customized to provide additional detail about population count by different categories:

*   Urban vs. rural
*   Race/ethnicity
*   Age groups

[**From the U.S. Census Bureau:**](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/about/glossary.html#par_textimage_13)

**"Block Groups (BGs)** are statistical divisions of census tracts, are generally defined to contain between 600 and 3,000 people, and are used to present data and control block numbering. A block group consists of clusters of blocks within the same census tract that have the same first digit of their four-digit census block number.

**Census Tracts** are small, relatively permanent statistical subdivisions of a county or statistically equivalent entity that can be updated by local participants prior to each decennial census as part of the Census Bureau’s Participant Statistical Areas Program (PSAP). The Census Bureau delineates census tracts in situations where no local participant responded or where state, local, or tribal governments declined to participate. The primary purpose of census tracts is to provide a stable set of geographic units for the presentation of statistical data.

Census tracts generally have a population size between 1,200 and 8,000 people, with an optimum size of 4,000 people."

## About the Data Quality

The 2020 Census has numerous quality checks built into data collection and data processing. After the data are released, we continue to do an even deeper dive to evaluate the quality of the census in two major ways:

*   Looking at how well we conducted the census.
*   Comparing the census results to other ways of measuring the population, such as Demographic Analysis and Post-Enumeration Surveys.

*   [2020 Census Data Quality](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial-census/decade/2020/planning-management/process/data-quality.html "2020 Census Data Quality")

## About the Data Quality

The 2020 Census has numerous quality checks built into data collection and data processing. After the data are released, we continue to do an even deeper dive to evaluate the quality of the census in two major ways:

*   Looking at how well we conducted the census.
*   Comparing the census results to other ways of measuring the population, such as Demographic Analysis and Post-Enumeration Surveys.

*   [2020 Census Data Quality](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial-census/decade/2020/planning-management/process/data-quality.html "2020 Census Data Quality")

The **2020 United States census** was the 24th decennial [United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_census "United States census"). Census Day, the reference day used for the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census"), was April 1, 2020. Other than a pilot study during the [2000 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_census "2000 United States census"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-1) this was the first U.S. census to offer options to respond online or by phone, in addition to the paper response form used for previous censuses.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-auto-2)

The census was taken during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), which affected its administration. The census recorded a resident population of 331,449,281 in the 50 states and the national capital of [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), reflecting an increase of 7.4%, or 22,703,743, over [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-3) The growth rate was the second-lowest ever recorded, and the net increase was the sixth-highest in history. This was the first census where the ten most-populous states each surpassed ten million residents, and the first census where the ten most-populous cities each surpassed one million residents.

This census's data determined the electoral votes' distribution for the [2024 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election"). A subsequent review by the [Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") found significant miscounts in several minority populations and in several states.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/2020_US_Census_Yard_Sign.jpg/250px-2020_US_Census_Yard_Sign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020_US_Census_Yard_Sign.jpg)

A 2020 U.S. census yard sign in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio")

As required by the [United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States"), the U.S. census has been conducted every 10 years since 1790. The 2010 United States census was the previous census completed. All people in the U.S. 18 and older are legally obligated to answer census questions, and to do so truthfully ([Title 13 of the United States Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_13_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 13 of the United States Code")).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-5)[Personally identifiable information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data "Personal data") is private and the Census Bureau itself will never release it. However, the [National Archives and Records Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_and_Records_Administration "National Archives and Records Administration") could release the original census returns in 2092, if the [72-year rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau#Data_stewardship "United States Census Bureau") is not changed before then.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-6)

On census reference day, April 1, 2020, the resident United States population (50 states and Washington, D.C., excluding overseas territories and military members and civilian U.S. citizens living abroad) was projected to be 329.59 million,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-7) a 6.76% increase from the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census").

## Purpose

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Purpose")]

### Reapportionment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Reapportionment")]

See also: [United States congressional apportionment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment "United States congressional apportionment")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/2020_census_reapportionment.svg/250px-2020_census_reapportionment.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020_census_reapportionment.svg)

Allocation of [U.S. congressional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") districts following the 2020 census

The results of the 2020 census determine the number of seats for each state in the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), hence also the number of electors for each state in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), for elections from 2022 to 2032.

The Census Bureau announced the apportionment figures on April 26, 2021. 13 states had changes in congressional seats:

*   [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia") lost one seat.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-8)
*   [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), and [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon") gained one seat.
*   [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") gained two seats.

This represented a smaller number of seats shifting than was forecast by independent analysts.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-9)

### Redistricting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Redistricting")]

See also: [2020 United States redistricting cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_redistricting_cycle "2020 United States redistricting cycle")

State and local officials use censuses to redraw boundaries for districts such as congressional districts ([redistricting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redistricting "Redistricting")), state legislative districts, and school districts.

### Federal funding distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Federal funding distribution")]

Dozens of federal programs use census data to help direct funding to state and local areas. Census results help determine how more than $675 billion in federal funding are allocated to states and communities each year for roads, schools, hospitals (health clinics), emergency services, and more.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-10)

## Major design changes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Major design changes")]

The 2020 census was the first U.S. census to offer a full internet response option and the first to extensively use technology instead of paper to manage and conduct fieldwork.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-11)

Key design changes included:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-auto-2)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-12)

*   Three response options: Internet, paper, and phone. Ultimately, every household that did not respond online was sent a paper form. Households in areas with low internet access received a paper form from the start.
*   Multiple languages: In addition to English, respondents were able to complete the census in 12 other languages online or by phone; in addition, language guides, language glossaries, and language identification cards were provided in 59 non-English languages.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-16)
*   In-office address canvassing: In the 2010 and earlier censuses, census workers walked every street in the United States to verify addresses on the ground. The 2020 census used [satellite imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_imagery "Satellite imagery") and [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPS "GPS") to identify areas where housing had changed and assigned workers to verify those addresses in person.
*   Digital case management: Census takers used secure [iPhone 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_8 "IPhone 8")[smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone")[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-17) to receive daily assignments, navigate to interviews, communicate with supervisors, and submit timesheets. Special software was designed to optimize assignments, streamline management, flag issues immediately, and reduce unnecessary follow-up visits.
*   Streamlined follow-up visits using existing data sources: The 2020 census used existing government and third-party data to identify vacant households, to predict the best time of day to visit a particular household, and to count and provide characteristics for the people in the household after multiple attempts using existing high-quality data from trusted sources.

## Questions and data uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Questions and data uses")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/2020_census_questionnaire.jpg/250px-2020_census_questionnaire.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020_census_questionnaire.jpg)

Copies of the 2020 census questionnaire

As required by the Census Act,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-18) the U.S. Census Bureau submitted a list of questions to Congress on March 29, 2018.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-n598018163-19) The U.S. census will not share any participant's information with any government agency, as it is prohibited by Title 13 United States code. It has been challenged, but the Supreme Court has always prevailed in reference to Title 13 to protect the confidentiality and privacy of information provided.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-20) Based on those questions and a subsequent executive order, the 2020 census asked:[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-CNN_July_2019-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-22)

1.   The number of people living or staying at the respondent's home on April 1, 2020. Used for the total count and to ensure everyone is counted once, only once, and in the right place according to where they live on Census Day.
2.   Whether the home is owned or rented. Used to produce statistics about homeownership and renters for economic indicators, housing programs and informing planning decisions.
3.   The sex of each person in the household. Used to produce statistics used to plan and fund government programs, enforce laws, regulations, and policies against discrimination.
4.   The age of each person in the household. Used to better understand the size and characteristics of different age groups. Agencies use these data to plan and fund government programs that support specific age groups, including children and older populations.
5.   The race of each person in the household. Used by federal agencies to monitor compliance with anti-discrimination provisions, such as those under the Voting Rights Act and the Civil Rights Act.
6.   Whether a person in the household is of Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish origin. Used by federal agencies to monitor compliance with anti-discrimination provisions, such as those under the Voting Rights Act and the Civil Rights Act.
7.   The relationship of each person in the household to each other. Used to plan and fund government programs that support families, including people raising children alone and other households who qualify for additional assistance.

The [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") proposed but then withdrew plans to add a new category to classify [Middle Eastern and North African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MENA "MENA") peoples, over a dispute over whether this classification should be considered a white ethnicity or a separate race.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-23)

*   January–March 2019: The U.S. Census Bureau opens 39 area census offices.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-auto-2)

*   January 21, 2020: The Census Bureau begins counting the population in remote Alaska, with [Toksook Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toksook_Bay "Toksook Bay") being the first town to be enumerated.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-25)
*   April 1, 2020: Census Day is observed nationwide. By this date, households received an invitation to participate in the 2020 census. There are three options for responding: online, by mail, or by phone.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-timeline-27)

*   May 2020: The Census Bureau begins following up with households who have not responded (NRFU [Nonresponse Followup] delayed to August 11–October 31). In August 2020, the 3-month NRFU enumeration period was compressed to two 1/2 months, ending October 15, 2020.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-28)
*   September 23–24: People experiencing homelessness counted by officials who visited shelters, at soup kitchens and mobile food vans, and non-sheltered, outdoor locations such as tent encampments.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-ImportantDates-29)
*   October 15: Self-response [data collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_collection "Data collection") ends with over 99.9% of households having self-responded or been counted by census takers.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-ImportantDates-29)
*   October 16, 2020: The count ends.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-NPR-30)
*   December 31, 2020: The Census Bureau delivers apportionment counts to the U.S. president.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-ImportantDates-29)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Anomalies-31) (This had been delayed to April 30, 2021).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-NCSL-32)

## Response rates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Response rates")]

According to the Census Bureau, 60.0% of all U.S. households had submitted their census questionnaire by May 22, 2020 –either online, by mail or by phone. Most U.S. households were mailed an invitation letter between March 12–20 to self-respond. They account for more than 95% of all U.S. households. Prior to the ongoing [coronavirus pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), the remaining 5% of U.S. households (mostly in rural areas) were supposed to be visited by census takers in April/May, dropping off invitation letters to owners. This was delayed, but most census offices restarted work again in mid-May. By July 14, 2020, the self-response rate was 62.1% or 91,800,000 households.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-36) The self-response rate was 66.5% in 2010 and 67.4% in 2000.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-99.98%_complete-37)

In an update published October 19, 2020, the Census Bureau stated 99.98% of addresses had been accounted for, with all but one state over a 99.9% rate. Paper responses postmarked on or before October 15 would be processed, as long as they arrived at the processing center by October 22.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-99.98%_complete-37)

## Marketing and partnerships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Marketing and partnerships")]

As in previous censuses, the 2020 census relied on a network of trusted voices nationwide to help raise awareness, answer questions, and encourage communities to participate.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-38) Hundreds of local "complete count committees" are dedicating resources to the efforts nationwide.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-40)

VMLY&R (formerly [Young & Rubicam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_&_Rubicam "Young & Rubicam")) secured the Integrated Communications Contract for the 2020 census campaign in August 2016.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-41) As the contract's primary agency of record, VMLY&R created an integrated team for this project, Team Y&R, which includes subcontractors specializing in minority outreach, digital media, [earned media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earned_media "Earned media") and more.

In March 2019, the campaign unveiled the 2020 census tagline: "Shape your future. START HERE." The tagline was based on research that demonstrated which types of messages will reach and motivate all populations, including segments of the population who are historically hard to count.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-43)

## COVID-19 pandemic emergency

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: COVID-19 pandemic emergency")]

On March 18, 2020, the [U.S. Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Census_Bureau "U.S. Census Bureau") issued a [press release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_release "Press release") by Director [Steven Dillingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Dillingham "Steven Dillingham") announcing that 2020 census field operations would be suspended for two weeks until April 1, 2020, due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-46) On March 27, 2020, the agency announced it would temporarily suspend in-person interviews for its on-going surveys.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-47) The agency claimed that staffing adjustments at its call centers due to implementing health guidance had "led to increases in call wait times, affecting different languages at different times".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-48) According to its own documentation, the U.S. Census Bureau continued to pay 2020 census employees even though field operations were supposed to be suspended.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-49)

On March 28, 2020, the U.S. Census Bureau issued another press release announcing 2020 census field operations would be suspended for an additional two weeks, through April 15, 2020.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-50) Census Bureau officials communicated to the media that on March 27, 2020, they learned an employee had tested positive for COVID-19 at the agency's National Processing Center in Jeffersonville, Indiana,[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-51) which the agency kept open during the suspension, claiming they would "transition to the minimum number of on-site staff necessary to continue operations".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Jeffersonville_Statement-52) The agency announced on April 10, 2020, that it took steps to make "more employees available to respond to requests" at the call centers.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-53)

In a joint statement on April 13, 2020, [U.S. Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce") secretary [Wilbur Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ross "Wilbur Ross") and U.S. Census Bureau director Steven Dillingham announced further operational adjustments to the 2020 census due to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") health and safety concerns.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-COVID_Adjustments-54) In the statement, it was explained that "steps [were] being taken to reactivate field offices beginning June 1, 2020", "in-person activities, including all interaction with the public, enumeration, office work and processing activities, [would] incorporate the most current guidance to promote the health and safety of staff and the public" including "[personal protective equipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_protective_equipment "Personal protective equipment") (PPE) and [social distancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_distancing "Social distancing") practices".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-COVID_Adjustments-54) This release stated "in order to ensure the completeness and accuracy of the 2020 census, the Census Bureau is seeking statutory relief from [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") of 120 additional calendar days to deliver final [apportionment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment "United States congressional apportionment") counts"[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-COVID_Adjustments-54) due to the COVID-19 emergency, and that "under this plan, the Census Bureau would extend the window for field data collection and self-response to October 31, 2020, which will allow for apportionment counts to be delivered to the president by April 30, 2021, and redistricting data to be delivered to the states no later than September 30, 2021."[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-COVID_Adjustments-54)

On April 15, 2020, U.S. Census Bureau director Steven Dillingham wrote to Department of Commerce [inspector general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector_general "Inspector general") Peggy E. Gustafson responding to a March 12, 2020, memo sent by the [Office of the Inspector General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Inspector_General_(United_States) "Office of Inspector General (United States)") requesting information about the Census Bureau's plans to respond to the COVID-19 emergency by March 20, 2020.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-55) The inspector general's memo asked how the Bureau would address staff and enumerator safety. Dillingham's April 15 letter:

> The Census Bureau is closely coordinating the acquisition of needed PPE materials for field and office staff through the Department of Commerce's Coronavirus Taskforce. Federal partners include the Department of Homeland Security and the Centers for Disease Control. We have generated and submitted estimates for equipment needs. On April 15, 2020, the Agency's internal task force met and discussed our estimates for needed equipment, potential delivery dates, and budget implications. We continue to monitor the situation and make adjustments as necessary.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

To ensure the completeness and accuracy of the 2020 census, the Census Bureau is seeking statutory relief from Congress of 120 additional calendar days to deliver final apportionment counts.

Under this plan, the Census Bureau would extend the window for field data collection and self-response to October 31, 2020, which will allow for apportionment counts to be delivered to the President by April 30, 2021, and redistricting data to be delivered to the states no later than September 30, 2021.

On April 24, 2020, Dillingham and other Census Bureau officials briefed the [House Committee on Oversight and Reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Oversight_and_Reform "United States House Committee on Oversight and Reform") on the agency's response to the COVID-19 emergency.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Coronavirus_Brief-56) This briefing came after many requests from the committee since March 12, 2020,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-57) including a last-minute cancellation on April 20, 2020.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-58) In the briefing, [Albert E. Fontenot Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_E._Fontenot_Jr.?action=edit&redlink=1 "Albert E. Fontenot Jr. (page does not exist)"), the associate director for decennial census programs, explained that the bureau was planning a "phased start to many of our census operations" rather than beginning field operations nationwide on June 1, 2020, as previously announced and said operations would resume at different times in different areas of the country based on federal, state, and local public health guidance, as well as the availability of personal protective equipment, prioritizing reopening mail processing centers and census offices and said the bureau would notify Congress as it begins to restart operations.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Coronavirus_Brief-56) However, the National Processing Center and Area Census Offices had remained open.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Jeffersonville_Statement-52)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-59)

Starting on May 4, 2020, the U.S. Census Bureau began publishing dates as it claimed to begin a "phased restart of some 2020 census field operations in select geographic areas" and said they had "ordered personal protective equipment (PPE) for all field staff, including those that work in a field office. These materials will be secured and provided to staff prior to restarting operations."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Bureau_resumes_operations-60) Publicly published [procurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procurement "Procurement") data shows that an award was signed on April 28, 2020, for non-medical, reusable face masks for area census offices in a $5,001,393.60 contract awarded to [Industries for the Blind and Visually Impaired, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skilcraft "Skilcraft")[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-61) Around that time, two contracts for hand sanitizer were awarded to [Travis Association for the Blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Association_for_the_Blind "Travis Association for the Blind"), one signed on May 9, 2020, in a $57,390.00 contract[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FPDS-NG_ezSearch-62) and the other signed on May 13, 2020, in a $557,251.20 contract,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FPDS-NG_ezSearch_2-63) with both contracts listing the place of principal performance as Jeffersonville, Indiana.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FPDS-NG_ezSearch-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FPDS-NG_ezSearch_2-63) The agency decided that [face shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_shield "Face shield") were necessary to protect employees from COVID-19 exposure, but provided them only to personnel at the headquarters and national processing centers.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-64) An [OSHA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") complaint was made from [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City") on May 1, 2020, complaining that employees were not able to practice social distancing and were not provided with adequate personal protective equipment such as gloves and masks,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FOIA-65) showing the office was open prior to the Census Bureau's published office restart date of May 4, 2020.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Bureau_resumes_operations-60)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Release_4_August_2020-66)

Additional "restart" dates starting May 18 were published on May 15, 2020, for other geographic areas in eleven states.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-67) An OSHA complaint was recorded that same day from [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), that desks remained close together with no physical dividers, improper sanitation practices were being used, and no [remote work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_work "Remote work") for high-risk employees.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FOIA-65) The published restart date for the St. Louis Area Census Office was May 11, 2020.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Release_4_August_2020-66)

On May 21, 2020, procurement information for two contracts was entered into the [Federal Procurement Data System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Procurement_Data_System "Federal Procurement Data System"). One contract was for $1,502,928.00 awarded to [Industries for the Blind and Visually Impaired, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skilcraft "Skilcraft") for hand sanitizer,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-68) and a contract for $7,053,569.85 for four-ounce (118 ml) hand sanitizers awarded to NewView Oklahoma, Inc.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-69) both with the place of principal performance listed as [Jeffersonville, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffersonville,_Indiana "Jeffersonville, Indiana").

May 22, 2020, saw two additional contracts, one was a disinfectant wipes contract for $3,137,533.00 awarded to [Industries for the Blind and Visually Impaired, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skilcraft "Skilcraft")[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-70) and the other was a contract for $2,107,000.00 awarded to NewView Oklahoma for blue nitrile gloves, both with a place of principal performance listed as Jeffersonville, Indiana.

A press release on May 22, 2020, announced May 25 "restart" dates for ten more states.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Bureau_resumes_May_22_2020-71) An [OSHA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupational_Safety_and_Health_Administration "Occupational Safety and Health Administration") complaint was made from [Concord, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord,_California "Concord, California"), on April 3, 2020, that there were at least two confirmed cases of COVID-19 unrecorded on OSHA 300 logs and that employees were working in close quarters with no disinfection of shared equipment such as headsets, laptops, and tablets.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FOIA-65) The published restart date for the Concord, California, Area Census Office was May 25, 2020.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Bureau_resumes_May_22_2020-71)

Offices were reopened in the areas of "[American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), the [Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands"), [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam") and the [U.S. Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands") in preparation for resuming operations for the 2020 Island Areas Censuses" on May 22, 2020.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-72)

On May 29, 2020, a press release was published announcing "restart" of operations in seven additional states and the Washington, D.C., area starting from the week of June 1.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Bureau_resumes_May_29_2020-73) An OSHA complaint was made from [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"), on May 27, 2020, complaining that [CDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") guidelines were not being followed, that employees were unable to practice social distancing, and that employees experiencing flu-like symptoms and positive COVID-19 test results continued to come to work,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-FOIA-65) showing the office was open prior to the Census Bureau's published office restart date of June 1, 2020.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Bureau_resumes_May_29_2020-73)

In a June 5, 2020, press release, the U.S. Census Bureau announced additional area census offices (ACOs) would "restart" on June 8, saying that with "these additions, field activities have restarted in 247 of 248 area census offices stateside, all ACOs in Puerto Rico and the island areas, and 98.9% of the nation's update leave workload will have resumed."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-74) The June 5 press release was reissued on June 9, 2020, which included the addition of a June 11 "restart" at the [Window Rock, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Window_Rock,_Arizona "Window Rock, Arizona"), Area Census Office.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-75) Days later, the Navajo Nation began reinstating lockdown restrictions and curfews due to a surge in new cases.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-77)

A June 12, 2020, press release shared that the update leave (UL) operation had resumed, as well as fingerprinting of selected applicants.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Updates_June_2020-78) The agency announced that the update enumerate (UE) operation would restart on June 14 "in remote parts of northern Maine and [southeast Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Alaska "Southeast Alaska")" where employees update the Census Bureau's address list and interview households for the 2020 census, claiming "all census takers have been trained on social distancing protocols, and will be issued personal protective equipment (PPE) and will follow local guidelines for their use."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Updates_June_2020-78) The June 12 press release also shared that the communications campaign had been adapted due to the pandemic and would continue through October, "the end of 2020 census data collection operations", with additional paid media planned for July, August and September,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Updates_June_2020-78) though a July 15 list of media vendors showed only plans through the end of July.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-79)

On August 3, 2020, the Census Bureau announced that field collection would end on September 30, rather than October 31 as planned in April.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-81) In a leaked internal document, Census Bureau career officials determined that starting Nonresponse Followup Operations in this Replan would put the health and safety of employees at risk, stating, "These ACOs will have to deploy staff regardless of the COVID-19 risk in those areas to open on these dates."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-82) On September 8, 2020, Mark H. Zabarsky, Principal Assistant Inspector General for Audit and Evaluation published an alert on behalf of the Department of Commerce Office of Inspector General, which stated that the number of COVID-19 related safety issues raised by hotline complaints tripled between July 1 and August 21.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-83)

## Citizenship question debate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Citizenship question debate")]

The U.S. decennial census is used to determine federal funds, grants, and support to states. The Census Bureau had included a citizenship question until 1950 when it was removed, though it continued to include a question asking about place of birth.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-86) In a January 2018 memo, an initial evaluation by Census Bureau officials advised against such a question, saying that compiling citizenship data from existing administrative records is more accurate and far less expensive; however, [Wilbur Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilbur_Ross "Wilbur Ross"), [secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_Commerce "Secretary of Commerce") of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce") which oversees the Census Bureau, decided the administrative approach alone would not be sufficient.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-87) The Census Bureau announced in March 2018 its plan to add a question related to citizenship for the 2020 census: "Is this person a citizen of the United States?"[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-n598018163-19)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Questions_Planned-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-89) For the 2020 census, Ross told Congress the citizenship numbers were necessary to enforce the [Voting Rights Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act "Voting Rights Act")'s protection against voting discrimination.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-Questions_Planned-88) Ross was accused by Democrats in Congress of lying that the citizenship question was requested by the Justice Department and approved by him.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-91)

Upon the bureau's announcement, several state and city officials criticized the decision, reiterating the concern about discouraging participation from immigrants, resulting in undercounting, and questioning the motives of Secretary Ross in adding the question. Three simultaneous separate federal lawsuits came out of this discovery, occurring at the district courts of New York, Maryland, and California.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-3_district-92) During the controversy over the census question, the Census Bureau ran a test census in June 2019 on about 480,000 households to determine what effects adding the census question would have on participation, and to prepare the bureau, its staffing, and its counting measurements, to handle the potential lack of responses due to the citizenship question.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-93)

During these trials, documents released in May 2019 showed that the late [Thomas B. Hofeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_B._Hofeller "Thomas B. Hofeller"), an architect of Republican [gerrymandering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrymandering_in_the_United_States "Gerrymandering in the United States"), had found that adding the census question could help to gerrymander maps that "would be advantageous to Republicans and non-Hispanic whites".[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-nytimes_hofeller-94) Hofeller later wrote the DOJ letter which justified the policy by claiming it was needed to enforce the 1965 Voting Rights Act.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-nytimes_hofeller-94) Following this discovery, the [United States House Committee on Oversight and Reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Oversight_and_Reform "United States House Committee on Oversight and Reform") issued subpoenas for the Department of Justice to provide materials related to the censu

The **2020 United States census** was the 24th decennial [United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_census "United States census"). Census Day, the reference day used for the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census "Census"), was April 1, 2020. Other than a pilot study during the [2000 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_census "2000 United States census"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-1) this was the first U.S. census to offer options to respond online or by phone, in addition to the paper response form used for previous censuses.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-auto-2)

The census was taken during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), which affected its administration. The census recorded a resident population of 331,449,281 in the 50 states and the national capital of [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), reflecting an increase of 7.4%, or 22,703,743, over [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-3) The growth rate was the second-lowest ever recorded, and the net increase was the sixth-highest in history. This was the first census where the ten most-populous states each surpassed ten million residents, and the first census where the ten most-populous cities each surpassed one million residents.

This census's data determined the electoral votes' distribution for the [2024 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election"). A subsequent review by the [Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") found significant miscounts in several minority populations and in several states.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/2020_US_Census_Yard_Sign.jpg/250px-2020_US_Census_Yard_Sign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020_US_Census_Yard_Sign.jpg)

A 2020 U.S. census yard sign in [Columbus, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus,_Ohio "Columbus, Ohio")

As required by the [United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States"), the U.S. census has been conducted every 10 years since 1790. The 2010 United States census was the previous census completed. All people in the U.S. 18 and older are legally obligated to answer census questions, and to do so truthfully ([Title 13 of the United States Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_13_of_the_United_States_Code "Title 13 of the United States Code")).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-5)[Personally identifiable information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data "Personal data") is private and the Census Bureau itself will never release it. However, the [National Archives and Records Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_and_Records_Administration "National Archives and Records Administration") could release the original census returns in 2092, if the [72-year rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau#Data_stewardship "United States Census Bureau") is not changed before then.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-6)

On census reference day, April 1, 2020, the resident United States population (50 states and Washington, D.C., excluding overseas territories and military members and civilian U.S. citizens living abroad) was projected to be 329.59 million,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-7) a 6.76% increase from the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census").

### Reapportionment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Reapportionment")]

See also: [United States congressional apportionment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_congressional_apportionment "United States congressional apportionment")

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/2020_census_reapportionment.svg/250px-2020_census_reapportionment.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020_census_reapportionment.svg)

Allocation of [U.S. congressional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") districts following the 2020 census

The results of the 2020 census determine the number of seats for each state in the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), hence also the number of electors for each state in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College "United States Electoral College"), for elections from 2022 to 2032.

The Census Bureau announced the apportionment figures on April 26, 2021. 13 states had changes in congressional seats:

*   [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia "West Virginia") lost one seat.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-8)
*   [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), and [Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon "Oregon") gained one seat.
*   [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") gained two seats.

This represented a smaller number of seats shifting than was forecast by independent analysts.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-9)

State and local officials use censuses to redraw boundaries for districts such as congressional districts ([redistricting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redistricting "Redistricting")), state legislative districts, and school districts.

### Federal funding distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Federal funding distribution")]

Dozens of federal programs use census data to help direct funding to state and local areas. Census results help determine how more than $675 billion in federal funding are allocated to states and communities each year for roads, schools, hospitals (health clinics), emergency services, and more.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-10)

## Major design changes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Major design changes")]

The 2020 census was the first U.S. census to offer a full internet response option and the first to extensively use technology instead of paper to manage and conduct fieldwork.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-11)

Key design changes included:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-auto-2)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-12)

*   Three response options: Internet, paper, and phone. Ultimately, every household that did not respond online was sent a paper form. Households in areas with low internet access received a paper form from the start.
*   Multiple languages: In addition to English, respondents were able to complete the census in 12 other languages online or by phone; in addition, language guides, language glossaries, and language identification cards were provided in 59 non-English languages.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-16)
*   In-office address canvassing: In the 2010 and earlier censuses, census workers walked every street in the United States to verify addresses on the ground. The 2020 census used [satellite imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_imagery "Satellite imagery") and [GPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPS "GPS") to identify areas where housing had changed and assigned workers to verify those addresses in person.
*   Digital case management: Census takers used secure [iPhone 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_8 "IPhone 8")[smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone "Smartphone")[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-17) to receive daily assignments, navigate to interviews, communicate with supervisors, and submit timesheets. Special software was designed to optimize assignments, streamline management, flag issues immediately, and reduce unnecessary follow-up visits.
*   Streamlined follow-up visits using existing data sources: The 2020 census used existing government and third-party data to identify vacant households, to predict the best time of day to visit a particular household, and to count and provide characteristics for the people in the household after multiple attempts using existing high-quality data from trusted sources.

## Questions and data uses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Questions and data uses")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/2020_census_questionnaire.jpg/250px-2020_census_questionnaire.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2020_census_questionnaire.jpg)

Copies of the 2020 census questionnaire

As required by the Census Act,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-18) the U.S. Census Bureau submitted a list of questions to Congress on March 29, 2018.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-n598018163-19) The U.S. census will not share any participant's information with any government agency, as it is prohibited by Title 13 United States code. It has been challenged, but the Supreme Court has always prevailed in reference to Title 13 to protect the confidentiality and privacy of information provided.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-20) Based on those questions and a subsequent executive order, the 2020 census asked:[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-CNN_July_2019-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-22)

1.   The number of people living or staying at the respondent's home on April 1, 2020. Used for the total count and to ensure everyone is counted once, only once, and in the right place according to where they live on Census Day.
2.   Whether the home is owned or rented. Used to produce statistics about homeownership and renters for economic indicators, housing programs and informing planning decisions.
3.   The sex of each person in the household. Used to produce statistics used to plan and fund government programs, enforce laws, regulations, and policies against discrimination.
4.   The age of each person in the household. Used to better understand the size and characteristics of different age groups. Agencies use these data to plan and fund government programs that support specific age groups, including children and older populations.
5.   The race of each person in the household. Used by federal agencies to monitor compliance with anti-discrimination provisions, such as those under the Voting Rights Act and the Civil Rights Act.
6.   Whether a person in the household is of Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish origin. Used by federal agencies to monitor compliance with anti-discrimination provisions, such as those under the Voting Rights Act and the Civil Rights Act.
7.   The relationship of each person in the household to each other. Used to plan and fund government programs that support families, including people raising children alone and other households who qualify for additional assistance.

The [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau") proposed but then withdrew plans to add a new category to classify [Middle Eastern and North African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MENA "MENA") peoples, over a dispute over whether this classification should be considered a white ethnicity or a separate race.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-23)

## Response rates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Response rates")]

According to the Census Bureau, 60.0% of all U.S. households had submitted their census questionnaire by May 22, 2020 –either online, by mail or by phone. Most U.S. households were mailed an invitation letter between March 12–20 to self-respond. They account for more than 95% of all U.S. households. Prior to the ongoing [coronavirus pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), the remaining 5% of U.S. households (mostly in rural areas) were supposed to be visited by census takers in April/May, dropping off invitation letters to owners. This was delayed, but most census offices restarted work again in mid-May. By July 14, 2020, the self-response rate was 62.1% or 91,800,000 households.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-36) The self-response rate was 66.5% in 2010 and 67.4% in 2000.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-99.98%_complete-37)

In an update published October 19, 2020, the Census Bureau stated 99.98% of addresses had been accounted for, with all but one state over a 99.9% rate. Paper responses postmarked on or before October 15 would be processed, as long as they arrived at the processing center by October 22.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-99.98%_complete-37)

## Marketing and partnerships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_United_States_census&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Marketing and partnerships")]

As in previous censuses, the 2020 census relied on a network of trusted voices nationwide to help raise awareness, answer questions, and encourage communities to participate.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-38) Hundreds of local "complete count committees" are dedicating resources to the efforts nationwide.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-40)

VMLY&R (formerly [Young & Rubicam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_&_Rubicam "Young & Rubicam")) secured the Integrated Communications Contract for the 2020 census campaign in August 2016.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-41) As the contract's primary agency of record, VMLY&R created an integrated team for this project, Team Y&R, which includes subcontractors specializing in minority outreach, digital media, [earned media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earned_media "Earned media") and more.

In March 2019, the campaign unveiled the 2020 census tagline: "Shape your future. START HERE." The tagline was based on research that demonstrated which types of messages will reach and motivate all populations, including segments of the population who are historically hard to count.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census#cite_note-43)
